sections.text:
World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood.

We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude.

Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning.

Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers.

Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs.

The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.

summary.en: The paper examines high-norm spatial outliers in World Action Model representations and reports that their action relevance persists after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their magnitude. It introduces RegisterWAM, adding learnable non-spatial registers for action conditioning, and pairs them with observation flow-matching supervision to suppress spatial outliers and concentrate responses in registers. A noised-observation objective is also introduced for recovering the current scene from corrupted inputs. The authors report benchmark success rates and improved real-world manipulation performance.

sections.text:
Robot manipulation has traditionally relied on end-effector-centric interactions. In contrast, humans routinely exploit whole-arm contacts to improve efficiency, robustness, and adaptability, especially when the hands are occupied or when precise grasping is unnecessary.

Enabling similar capabilities in robots remains challenging: the robot must select where on its arm to make contact, generate effective non-prehensile interactions, and satisfy task-specific pose or safety constraints on the end-effector.

We propose Whole-Arm Contact Learning (WACL), a hierarchical framework that describes each whole-arm contact task with three robot-agnostic representations and hands them to a quasi-static surface-contact optimizer: semantic keypoints that summarize the scene, a reference contact trajectory that specifies where and how the arm presses on the object, and safety-aware path constraints that a vision-language model generates from the task description to protect the end-effector's task.

The robot's kinematic chain enters only in this optimizer, which grounds these representations onto the arm by jointly searching over which link makes contact, where on that link, and the joint configuration that realizes it.

This decomposition lets WACL learn the contact trajectory from 10 bare-hand human demonstrations per task collected without teleoperation, while new end-effector constraints change only the optimizer's input rather than any trained component.

Real-world experiments on a 7-DoF arm across four whole-arm tasks show that WACL sustains contact under end-effector constraints where a strong link-pose baseline fails (78% vs. 33% success) and generalizes to new constraints without retraining. Website: https://wacl-robot.github.io

summary.en: The paper proposes Whole-Arm Contact Learning (WACL), which gives a quasi-static surface-contact optimizer scene keypoints, a contact trajectory learned from human demonstrations, and end-effector safety path constraints generated from task descriptions by a vision-language model. The optimizer incorporates the robot's kinematics to search for a contacting link, contact location, and joint configuration. The authors say each task uses 10 non-teleoperated bare-hand demonstrations. In real-world tests across four tasks on a 7-DoF arm, WACL reports 78% success under constraints versus 33% for a baseline, and generalization to new constraints without retraining.

sections.text:
Robust proprioceptive state estimation is crucial for legged robots, particularly in challenging environments where exteroceptive sensors are unreliable.

While traditional leg odometry typically relies on a single body-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) fused with leg kinematics via an extended Kalman filter (EKF), such methods are vulnerable to linearization errors and hard-contact assumptions, leading to severe drift during slippage or dynamic locomotion.In this paper, we propose LAG-IO, a factor graph-based multi-IMU state estimation framework that tightly couples measurements from a main body IMU, multiple leg-mounted IMUs, and joint encoders within a sliding-window optimization.

To handle non-stationary foot-ground interactions, we introduce a continuous probabilistic contact detection module based on kernel density estimation (KDE), which adaptively scales the covariance of zero-velocity update (ZUPT) factors.

Furthermore, kinematic relative position factors are formulated to structurally anchor the independent leg inertial states to the robot's main body.

Experimental results on a quadruped robot across various unstructured terrains demonstrate that, compared to existing baselines, LAG-IO achieves higher planar trajectory accuracy, reduces unobservable vertical divergence, and provides smoother trajectory transitions during unstable contacts, while maintaining competitive attitude observability.

summary.en: The paper presents LAG-IO, a factor graph framework for legged-robot state estimation that combines body and leg IMUs with joint encoders in a sliding window. It uses kernel density estimation for continuous probabilistic contact detection and adapts zero-velocity factor covariance, while kinematic relative-position factors anchor leg inertial states to the body. Experiments on a quadruped across unstructured terrains report improved planar trajectory accuracy, less vertical divergence, and smoother transitions during unstable contacts than existing baselines.

sections.text:
Odometry estimation using light detection and ranging (LiDAR) and an inertial measurement unit (IMU), known as LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO), often suffers from performance degradation in degenerate environments, such as long corridors or single-wall scenarios with narrow field-of-view LiDAR.

To address this limitation, we propose ALIVE-LIO, a degeneracy-aware LiDAR-inertial odometry framework that explicitly enhances state estimation in degenerate directions. The key contribution of ALIVE-LIO is the strategic integration of a deep neural network into a classical error-state Kalman filter (ESKF) to compensate for the loss of LiDAR observability.

Specifically, ALIVE-LIO employs a neural network to predict the body-frame velocity and selectively fuses this prediction into the ESKF only when degeneracy is detected, providing effective state updates along degenerate directions.

This design enables ALIVE-LIO to utilize the probabilistic structure and consistency of the ESKF while benefiting from learning-based motion estimation. The proposed method was evaluated on publicly available datasets exhibiting degeneracy, as well as on our own collected data.

Experimental results demonstrate that ALIVE-LIO substantially reduces pose drift in degenerate environments, yielding the top-ranked result in 22 out of 32 sequences. Our code is available at https://github.com/cocel-postech/alive-lio.

summary.en: The paper presents ALIVE-LIO, a LiDAR-inertial odometry framework for degenerate settings such as long corridors and single-wall scenes. A neural network predicts body-frame velocity, which is selectively fused into an error-state Kalman filter when degeneracy is detected, to compensate along poorly observable directions. The authors report that experiments on public datasets exhibiting degeneracy and their own collected data show reduced pose drift, with top-ranked results in 22 of 32 sequences.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map observations to actions with no objective that accounts for how the world responds, so their robustness is bounded primarily by data coverage.

World models carry precisely that missing objective and are better grounded for it, yet rolling the future forward costs seconds per decision and rules them out of the control loop. We show the two can be separated.

What a world model knows about physical scenes lives in its internal features; generating the future is merely the objective that produced them, so the grounding can be inherited while the generative machinery is left behind.

We add one feature-alignment term to ordinary VLA training: a frozen world model is run over the training frames once and cached, and the student learns to agree with that cache.

No teacher is loaded during training, the projector is discarded after it, and the deployed policy is identical to the undistilled baseline, running in 32ms and 1.86GB on a consumer RTX5090, so every gain is attributable to the representation rather than to added capacity or test-time compute.

A 0.8B student reaches 97.9% on LIBERO, improves from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1 humanoid manipulation, and the same objective carries over to real hardware, on both a single-arm and a bimanual platform.

The gain survives changes of student scale, backbone, alignment layer, and teacher, indicating a broad representational prior rather than a fragile alignment between two particular networks. Project page: https://thaw-vla.trung-dt.com/.

summary.en: The paper proposes distilling world-model representations into vision-language-action policies through a feature-alignment term. A frozen world model processes training frames once, and its cached features guide the student; the teacher and projector are absent at deployment. The authors say this transfers grounding without adding policy capacity or test-time compute. They report that a 0.8B student reaches 97.9% on LIBERO and improves from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1 manipulation. The abstract also says the objective carries over to real single-arm and bimanual hardware.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage.

Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts.

We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head.

Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth.

On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.

summary.en: The paper proposes Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL) for post-training vision-language-action policies. It jointly optimizes a policy and an online-updated simulator with a world model and reward proxy. Simulator reliability sets the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon, while chunk-level trust affects replay selection and optimization weights. A residual predictor estimates trust during recursive imagination without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, the authors report 79.7% average success and 10.9% faster high-threshold learning than a matched model-free control. Fixed-data adaptation with 50 demonstrations per task reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.

sections.text:
Leg odometry relies on the assumption that the velocity of a foot in stance is zero with respect to the world, which makes accurate contact detection a critical subproblem.

Many approaches classify contact using ground reaction force (GRF) sensors at the foot tip, yet these sensors are not available on all legged robots and remain unresponsive to disturbances such as slippage while the foot is still in contact.

Approaches without GRF sensing instead rely on heuristic pseudo-labels, model-based foot-velocity assumptions, or supervised contact learning.

In this study, we propose a self-supervised representation learning framework for contact detection that uses only standard proprioceptive sensing (joint encoders and IMU) and requires neither force sensors nor contact labels.

A denoising autoencoder is trained on kinematic features, a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model is fitted in the learned latent space, and its posterior is used as a continuous stance belief that scales the zero-velocity measurement covariance of an error-state Kalman filter.

Experiments in simulation and on real-world terrain show that our framework yields the lowest odometry error among supervised and probabilistic baselines, and that higher pseudo-label classification accuracy does not translate into better downstream odometry. Our code and dataset are publicly available.

summary.en: The paper proposes a self-supervised contact-detection representation framework using joint encoders and an IMU, without force sensors or contact labels. A denoising autoencoder learns from kinematic features, and a two-component Gaussian mixture model in latent space provides a continuous stance belief used to scale the zero-velocity measurement covariance in an error-state Kalman filter. The authors report the lowest odometry error among supervised and probabilistic baselines in simulation and real-world terrain experiments. They also report that better pseudo-label classification does not necessarily improve downstream odometry.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种仅使用关节编码器和惯性测量单元的自监督接触检测表示学习框架，不需要足端力传感器或接触标签。方法以运动学特征训练去噪自编码器，在潜在空间拟合双成分高斯混合模型，并用其后验概率形成连续支撑置信度，调节误差状态卡尔曼滤波器的零速度测量协方差。作者报告，该方法在仿真和真实地形实验中比所比较的监督及概率基线获得更低里程计误差；较高的伪标签分类准确率并未带来更好的下游里程计表现。

sections.text:
Video-to-robot pipelines for quadrupedal imitation insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. We present CopyQuad, which omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width instead.

The setting is side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion, where limb motion is almost entirely in the image plane. A frozen 2D keypoint detector and a fixed analytic retargeting then turn a single uncalibrated clip into a robot reference whose foot targets are reachable by construction, so no per-clip trajectory optimization is needed.

One phase-indexed reward structure, whose only per-behavior freedom is three scalars from a shared sweep, learns a dog walk, a horse walk, a horse trot and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware. We then measure what omitting the axis costs.

In a training-free rigidity test, a video depth model varies the distance between the animal's hips by $40$ to $107\%$ of its own mean and a single-image metric model by $22$ to $58\%$, though that distance cannot move.

Motion capture puts the true lateral paw travel of a dog walk at $4.5$ cm peak to peak, a mean deviation near $1.4$ cm against the $3.5$ cm of lateral foot error our policies already leave, so the discarded axis sits below the pipeline's resolution.

Depth repaired to feasibility never beats the constant, and the unrepaired estimates put the robot on the ground.

summary.en: CopyQuad converts a single uncalibrated side-view clip into quadruped robot references without a depth model or per-clip 3D reconstruction. It fixes the unseen lateral axis to the robot's stance width, then uses frozen 2D keypoints and analytic retargeting to produce reachable foot targets. The authors report learning dog and horse gaits and two non-periodic gestures with a shared phase-indexed reward structure, followed by zero-shot hardware deployment. Their rigidity test finds substantial variation in estimated hip distance, while measured lateral paw travel is small relative to existing policy foot error. Feasibility-repaired depth does not outperform the constant, and unrepaired estimates put the robot on the ground.
summary.zh: CopyQuad从单段未校准侧视视频生成四足机器人参考动作，不使用深度模型或逐片段三维重建，而是将不可见的横向轴固定为机器人自身站立宽度，并以二维关键点检测和解析重定向生成可达的足端目标。作者称，同一阶段索引奖励结构经共享参数搜索，学会狗步、马步、马小跑及两种非周期动作，并在硬件上零样本部署。测试显示，深度估计的髋部距离偏差较大；实测横向爪部移动低于策略已有横向足误差。修正深度未优于常数设定，未修正估计会使机器人落地。

sections.text:
This paper presents a geometry-aware predictive control framework for bipedal obstacle crossing across walking and running regimes. The proposed approach integrates a phase-structured trajectory generator with a constrained model predictive control (MPC) tracking layer to generate coordinated pelvis and swing-foot motions during obstacle traversal.

The crossing process is represented through five interpretable phases: pre-crossing, leading-leg clearance, straddle, trailing-leg clearance, and recovery.

Within this structure, swing-foot elevation is adapted as a function of obstacle height, while lateral stance widening and pelvis repositioning are introduced as functions of obstacle depth to improve transverse clearance and body alignment. A continuous gait-parameter evolution enables smooth walk-to-run transition without discrete controller switching.

The generated references are tracked using MPC to regulate motion smoothness, clearance feasibility, touchdown behavior, and lateral admissibility. The framework is evaluated in reduced-order simulation over five progressively difficult obstacles under walking and running conditions.

The robot successfully crosses the first four obstacles, achieving minimum body-obstacle clearances of 0.036, 0.036, 0.059, and 0.017 m, respectively. The fifth and most demanding obstacle leads to collision, identifying the current operating boundary of the proposed reduced-order formulation.

Overall, the method provides a compact, interpretable, and computationally efficient basis for intelligent obstacle-aware bipedal locomotion.

summary.en: The paper presents a geometry-aware predictive control framework for bipedal obstacle crossing while walking or running. A five-phase trajectory generator is paired with constrained model predictive control: swing-foot elevation varies with obstacle height, while stance widening and pelvis repositioning depend on obstacle depth. Continuous gait-parameter evolution supports smooth walk-to-run transitions. In reduced-order simulation across five progressively harder obstacles, the robot crosses the first four and collides with the fifth, which the authors identify as the current operating boundary of the formulation.

sections.text:
Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding.

We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call.

On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV.

On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success.

In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.

summary.en: TacitVLA is a vision-language-action model whose action expert does not attend to reasoning text generated during the current call. The authors argue that reasoning supervision improves the backbone representation, allowing actions to proceed without waiting for autoregressive reasoning. For long-horizon tasks, reasoning entries can be generated during execution as episodic memory. In a controlled evaluation across four manipulation and driving benchmarks, the authors report matching explicit-reasoning performance at up to 3.4 times lower latency, and matching the latency of a model trained without reasoning while improving success by up to 17.1%. The abstract also reports benchmark scores.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency.

We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop.

A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon.

We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite.

The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes.

These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/ylee-sling/Vision-Predictor-Action and https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/vpa-libero10, and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960920.

summary.en: The paper presents Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces token-by-token autoregressive action decoding with a latent control loop. It encodes observations, goal images, and instructions, selects a discrete skill, predicts the next latent state, and uses flow matching to generate an action chunk. The authors say sequential network evaluations per decision step do not grow with action horizon. In an initial LIBERO-10 proof of concept, trained from that suite’s demonstrations in a single run, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes; the authors describe the evidence as preliminary.
summary.zh: 论文提出目标条件化的 Vision-Predictor-Action（VPA），以轻量潜在控制循环替代逐词生成动作的自回归解码器。系统编码观测、目标图像和指令，选择离散技能，预测下一潜在状态，并用流匹配生成动作片段；作者称每步网络评估次数不随动作时域增长。初步概念验证在 LIBERO-10 上进行：模型仅用该套件演示训练，单次训练运行中，双摄像头策略在 200 个评估回合中成功率为 40.0%。这些结果被作者限定为初步证据，称方法可行。

sections.text:
A simulation of a real robot workspace must preserve task-relevant interactions, while policies developed in it must operate on observations available to the real robot. Yet scene reconstruction and policy development are often treated separately.

We present Agentic Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Agentic RSR), a framework that links scene reconstruction, policy development, and real-robot execution through the same manipulation task.

Given a workspace video, a task description, and a known robot model, an agent recovers metric scale, iteratively refines the scene using visual feedback, and checks task-relevant interactions in MuJoCo. A coding agent then develops an executable policy, progressing from privileged object poses to visual observations and randomized simulation.

The policy can interleave multiple observations and actions within one invocation, while the agent uses execution feedback to continue, retry, or revise its approach. A shared task-level interface carries the policy and accumulated experience to the real robot, where fresh observations and safety checks guide execution.

Using Claude Opus 5.5 through DeepSeek Harness (DSH), all 18 scenes across two robots pass the joint visual check; mean four-view Depth MAE against reference depth estimates is 0.0808 m, mean Lab $\Delta E_{76}$ is 8.01, and mean grayscale SSIM is 0.7338.

In real-robot experiments, the aggregate task success rate reaches 80% of the simulation task success rate, indicating substantial retention of simulated performance on hardware. Code and reconstructed scene data will be made publicly available.

summary.en: The paper presents Agentic RSR, linking scene reconstruction, policy development, and real-robot execution around the same manipulation task. From workspace video, a task description, and a known robot model, the framework recovers scale, refines the scene, and checks task-relevant interactions in MuJoCo. A coding agent develops policies using progressively less privileged observations and execution feedback. The authors report that all 18 scenes across two robots pass a joint visual check, and real-robot task success reaches 80% of simulation task success.
summary.zh: 论文提出 Agentic RSR，将场景重建、策略开发和真实机器人执行连接到同一操作任务中。框架从工作区视频、任务描述和已知机器人模型出发，恢复尺度并迭代细化场景，在 MuJoCo 中检查任务相关交互；编码代理逐步开发策略，并利用执行反馈调整方案。策略及累积经验通过共享任务接口转移到真实机器人，由新观测和安全检查指导执行。作者报告，两个机器人涉及的18个场景均通过联合视觉检查；真实机器人实验的任务成功率达到仿真任务成功率的80%。

sections.text:
Foundation-model (FM) based task and motion planning (TAMP) methods typically assume that the full scene is known before planning. In long-horizon manipulation, however, relevant objects may initially be hidden and only become observable as the robot interacts with the environment.

We introduce Robust-TAMP, a task and motion planning framework that first decides whether a discovery needs a replan. If replanning is needed, the robot executes unaffected actions while the FM synthesizes corrective actions.

These actions are inserted into the existing plan based on urgency, either executed immediately or deferred while preserving the remaining plan. We evaluate Robust-TAMP on 14 MuJoCo environments with hidden objects, blocked placements, articulated containers, and multi-step tasks, and on five real-world settings.

Our proposed method completes 92.1% of simulated tasks, outperforming four baseline comparison architectures by 47.1 percentage points under the same settings. Ablations show that each component either raises success or lowers planner calls, planning time, and robot idle time.

An extensive study across model sizes, text and vision inputs, reasoning modes, and prompting further shows that in-context examples help the planner follow multi-step procedures that zero-shot prompting struggles with. Our implementation code and project details are available at https://narendhiranv04.github.io/ROBUST-TAMP/.

summary.en: The paper introduces Robust-TAMP for deciding whether and how to replan during long-horizon manipulation when relevant objects are initially hidden. If replanning is needed, the robot can continue unaffected actions while a foundation model generates corrective actions, which are inserted immediately or deferred according to urgency. The authors evaluate the method in 14 MuJoCo environments and five real-world settings. They report 92.1% simulated task completion, 47.1 percentage points above four baselines under the same settings; ablations indicate components improve success or reduce planning costs and idle time.
summary.zh: 论文提出 Robust-TAMP，用于在物体初始隐藏、交互后才可见的长时程操作中决定是否以及如何重新规划。若需重规划，机器人可先执行不受影响的动作，同时由基础模型生成纠正动作；新动作按紧迫程度插入现有计划，可立即执行或延后。作者在14个 MuJoCo 环境和五种真实场景中评估，报告仿真任务完成率为92.1%，比相同设置下四种基线高47.1个百分点。消融研究显示，各组成部分可提升成功率或降低规划开销与机器人等待时间。

sections.text:
While expert demonstrations on real robots are difficult to collect, human ego-centric videos are easy to collect and abundant on the internet.

However, learning dexterous manipulation policies from human videos remains challenging---one of the most important challenges being the difficulty of reconstructing physically grounded robot trajectories due to the large embodiment gap.

In this paper, we propose EgoCPT, a novel paradigm for learning high-quality retargeted dexterous hand trajectories directly from an ego-centric video, which can then be deployed directly on real robots.

The only inputs to our method are an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand pose trajectory, which can be easily obtained through off-the-shelf software or specialized cameras during recording.

Our method is particularly robust to noisy hand poses attributed to our novel contact-aware optimization framework, which iteratively optimizes the contact points between the robot hands and objects.

Across five manipulation tasks, our method achieves overall success rates of 67.3% on noisy EgoDex hand-pose reconstructions and 92.0% on high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware, outperforming multiple baselines on both benchmarks.

summary.en: EgoCPT aims to produce robot dexterous-hand trajectories from a single egocentric video and a reference hand-pose trajectory, addressing the embodiment gap between human hands and robots. Its contact-aware optimization iteratively adjusts hand-object contact points to improve robustness to noisy poses. Across five manipulation tasks, the authors report overall success rates of 67.3% with noisy EgoDex reconstructions and 92.0% with high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware. These figures describe the reported benchmark evaluations.
summary.zh: EgoCPT旨在从单段第一视角视频和参考手部姿态轨迹中，重建可用于真实机器人的灵巧手操作轨迹，以应对人手与机器人之间的具身差异。方法通过迭代优化机器人手与物体的接触点，提高对噪声姿态的鲁棒性。作者报告，在五项操作任务中，使用噪声EgoDex姿态重建时总体成功率为67.3%，使用动作捕捉设备采集的高质量TACO重建时为92.0%；这些结果来自相应基准测试。

items.title: EgoCPT: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from a Single Ego-Centric Video with Contact-Aware Optimization

sections.text:
Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation.

Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity.

We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps.

These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .

summary.en: PrT-Flow is a flow-matching method for robot action policies that computes action probability densities while supporting multimodal, multi-step generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer makes sampling steps invertible, and Conditional Euler-step Training supervises their displacements. The authors prove that, under certain assumptions, this training objective has the same minimizers as fitting Flow Matching Euler-solver updates. They report 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 imitation-learning epochs and 96% on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600,000 online steps.
summary.zh: PrT-Flow为强化学习中的机器人动作策略提供可计算概率密度的流匹配方法，同时支持多模态、多步动作生成。其雅可比可计算变换器使采样步骤可逆，并便于计算雅可比行列式；条件Euler步训练监督采样步的位移。作者证明，在特定假设下，该训练目标与拟合流匹配Euler求解更新具有相同极小值。报告结果包括Robomimic Lift模仿学习成功率96%，以及OGBench Cube-Triple在线训练成功率96%。

items.title: PrT-Flow: Probability-Tractable Flow Matching for Reinforcement Learning

sections.text:
Likelihood-based policy gradient methods are the dominant approach for training robot control policies from rewards. These methods rely on differentiable action likelihoods, which constrain policy outputs to simple distributions like Gaussians.

In this work, we show how flow matching policy gradients, a recent framework that bypasses likelihood computation, can be made effective for training and finetuning more expressive policies in challenging robot control settings.

We introduce an improved objective that enables success in legged locomotion, humanoid motion tracking, and manipulation tasks, as well as robust sim-to-real transfer on two humanoid robots. We then present ablations and analysis on training dynamics.

Results show how policies can exploit the flow representation for exploration when training from scratch, as well as improved finetuning robustness over baselines.

summary.en: This work adapts flow-matching policy gradients, which bypass likelihood computation, to train and fine-tune expressive robot-control policies. The authors introduce an improved objective and report success in legged locomotion, humanoid motion tracking, and manipulation, as well as robust sim-to-real transfer on two humanoid robots. Their ablations and training-dynamics analysis indicate that policies can use the flow representation for exploration when trained from scratch, and that fine-tuning is more robust than the baselines. The abstract gives no specific success rates or experimental setup details.
summary.zh: 本文研究如何将流匹配策略梯度用于机器人控制策略训练与微调，以避免似然梯度方法对简单动作分布的依赖。作者提出改进目标，并报告其在腿式运动、人形动作跟踪和操作任务中取得成功，也在两台人形机器人上实现了稳健的仿真到现实迁移。消融与训练动态分析显示，从零开始训练时策略可利用流表示进行探索；与基线相比，微调的鲁棒性也有所提升。摘要未给出具体成功率或实验设置细节。

sections.text:
Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation.

To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning.

It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent.

Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions.

The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues.

We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.

summary.en: The paper proposes a hierarchical commander-executor framework for cooperative object manipulation by multiple humans or agents. The commander combines instructions and scene information, divides tasks into role-specific subtasks, and creates shared object-centered plans for timing, positions, and actions. Executors learn physics-based policies from local observations and high-level guidance through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum. Evaluations on varied tasks are reported to show long-horizon collaboration, scaling from two agents to multiple agents, and higher success rates than state-of-the-art methods.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种用于多人协作物体操作的指挥者—执行者分层框架。指挥者结合指令与场景信息进行语义和几何规划，将任务拆成按角色划分的子任务，并生成包含时序、目标位置和操作动作的共享物体中心计划；执行者依据该策略和各自局部观察，通过从单人到协作的课程学习物理策略。作者称，该方法在多种操作任务评估中能够完成长时序、多类型协作，并从双人扩展至多人，成功率高于现有先进方法。

items.title: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination

sections.text:
It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment.

As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone.

In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember.

IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency.

To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction.

Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs.

Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.

summary.en: The paper introduces IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework for vision-language-action models that does not explicitly constrain what the policy remembers. It incrementally compresses multiple streams, including observations, actions, and proprioception. Training first supervises memory reconstruction and task-progress estimation, then jointly fine-tunes the memory and policy for action prediction. Across memory-demanding simulation and real-world tasks, the authors report at least a 26% improvement in average success over the base VLA and the lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs.
summary.zh: 论文提出 IMPRINT，一种面向视觉—语言—动作模型的策略无关潜在记忆框架，无需显式规定策略应记住什么。它将观察、动作和本体感觉等多种信息流压缩为推理时增量更新的潜在记忆。训练分两阶段：先监督记忆重建过去信息并估计当前任务进度，再与策略端到端微调以预测动作。作者报告，在需要记忆的仿真和真实任务中，相比基础模型平均成功率至少提高26%，且在记忆增强型模型中推理延迟最低。

items.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies

sections.text:
Manipulation tasks such as unscrewing a cap or sliding a part in contact with a surface require imposing force along a high-friction direction: the robot must overcome a resistance rather than yield to it.

Generative visuomotor policies predict the motion for such tasks but not the authority needed to realize it, and that authority is bounded by the impedance controller beneath them: when the resistance exceeds what a compliant controller can exert under a bounded tracking error, the task is unattainable however accurate the prediction is.

The required amount cannot be anticipated either, since it depends on a contact state the observation does not reveal. In this paper, we propose a residual stiffening layer placed underneath an unmodified policy.

Resistance is recognized, without force sensing, from the mismatch between the motion the policy commands and the motion the robot realizes, and a four-mode supervisor raises the stiffness along a single direction read off the policy's own action chunk, retains it while the task progresses and releases it afterwards.

The layer needs no compliance labels, no retraining and no re-collected demonstrations.

On two real tasks, unscrewing a bottle cap and pushing a T-nut along a T-slot groove against non-homogeneous friction, evaluated at six resistance levels of which two were withheld from the demonstrations, the layer raises the success rate from 52% to 90% while producing 61% less peak off-axis force than a uniformly stiff controller at the same resistance.

summary.en: The paper proposes a residual stiffening layer beneath an existing visuomotor policy to handle unknown contact resistance. Without force sensing, it detects resistance from the mismatch between commanded and realized motion. A four-mode supervisor increases stiffness along a direction indicated by the policy's action chunk, maintains it as the task progresses, and later releases it. The authors report that the layer requires no compliance labels, retraining, or new demonstrations. On two real tasks tested at six resistance levels, including two withheld from demonstrations, success rises from 52% to 90%, while peak off-axis force is 61% lower than with a uniformly stiff controller at the same resistance.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种置于既有视觉运动策略下方的残差增刚层，用于应对未知接触阻力。该层不依赖力传感器，而是依据策略指令运动与机器人实际运动之间的偏差识别阻力，并由四模式监督器沿策略动作片段指示的方向调高刚度，在任务推进时保持、之后释放。作者称，该层无需柔顺性标签、重新训练或重新采集示范。在两个真实操作任务及六种阻力水平的评估中，其中两种未出现在示范里，成功率由52%升至90%，相较同阻力下均匀高刚度控制器，峰值离轴力减少61%。

items.title: Intent-guided Adaptive Stiffening for Visuomotor Policies under Unknown Resistance

The central challenge in reusing human actions across robots is the need to realize shared intent through incompatible kinematics, dynamics, and control interfaces.

We present SHARE, which decomposes action sharing into two connected stages---reference generation and feedback execution---and uses native robot references as their interface to achieve shared structure, native realization.

In the reference-generation stage, AdaMorph extracts human-motion intent with a shared temporal backbone and generates embodiment-compatible references through robot-conditioned decoding.

In the feedback-execution stage, AdaTrack combines these references with proprioception, action history, and morphology, then uses variable-length dynamic representations, morphology-conditioned attention, expert distillation, and closed-loop reinforcement learning to emit native actions from one shared Actor.

On G1, HI, AD, and T1, AdaMorph attains seen/unseen root-speed Pearson correlation coefficients (PCCs) of 0.951/0.894; AdaTrack reaches 94.00%/91.96% closed-loop Success Rate with 21.15% of the total parameters in four specialist Actors, while cross-embodiment pretraining improves seen/unseen adaptation by 9.67/13.62 points with only 1% target data.

summary.en: The paper presents SHARE, a framework that divides cross-robot action sharing into reference generation and feedback execution, using native robot references as the interface. AdaMorph extracts human-motion intent and generates embodiment-compatible references; AdaTrack combines them with proprioception, action history, and morphology to produce native actions from a shared Actor. The abstract reports correlation, closed-loop success, and adaptation results on G1, HI, AD, and T1, but does not specify whether these reported results are from simulation or physical experiments.

sections.text:
Quadruped robots deployed for inspection and field missions must cross heterogeneous terrain, from stairs, slopes, and gaps to high platforms, stepping stones, and balance beams, where safe support is sparse or see-through. Existing methods interpose a terrain map or a depth image between sensing and control.

Maps are costly to maintain, corrupted by odometry drift and outliers, and misled by see-through gratings, while depth cameras degrade with lighting and surface material.

In this paper, we present PointWalker, a mapless framework whose single reinforcement learning policy directly consumes raw point clouds from four light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors.

Voxelized points are encoded by linear self-attention and fused with proprioception through cross-attention, so terrain geometry reaches the policy without maps or foothold estimation.

One proximal policy optimization (PPO) run, with terrain-aware rewards and dual-channel simulation of see-through gratings, yields one policy for all seven terrain classes with a 90.1% mean success rate in simulation.

Deployed zero-shot on a Deep Robotics X30 at 50 Hz onboard, it crosses 0.8-m gaps, climbs 0.8-m platforms and 45{\deg} steel-grating stairs, carries a 50-kg payload, and completes a 2.5-km mountain route.

summary.en: The paper introduces PointWalker, a mapless quadruped locomotion framework that takes raw point clouds from four LiDAR sensors directly, without terrain maps or foothold estimation. Its reinforcement learning policy encodes voxelized points and fuses them with proprioception. A single PPO training run produces a policy for seven terrain classes, with a 90.1% mean success rate in simulation. The abstract also reports zero-shot deployment on a Deep Robotics X30 and describes performance on gaps, platforms, steel-grating stairs, payload carrying, and a mountain route.

sections.text:
Multi-robot systems (MRS) offer significant advantages over single-robot platforms by enabling information sharing and coordination for different tasks in complex environments.

However, reliable cooperation critically depends on inferring trust over both information sources and their reported hypotheses, particularly under partial observability and potential adversarial interference.

Existing approaches frequently depend on pre-established trust relationships or side-channel information, which may not be available or reliable in realistic MRS deployments.

This work introduces NeST-Bayes, a neural-symbolic framework that jointly infers robot and hypothesis trust using only inter-robot observation consistency, without requiring preassigned robot trust, reputation information, or side-channel identity signals.

NeST-Bayes infers instantaneous trust evidence scores for robots and object hypotheses by reasoning over ego-centric relational graphs constructed from cross-robot observation consistency. These evidence scores are accumulated over time through Bayesian updates of Beta-distributed trust beliefs to maintain temporally consistent trust estimates.

Extensive evaluations show that NeST-Bayes achieves the highest mean object precision and robot recall across all benchmark settings, and the highest robot precision and object recall in most settings, compared to trust-based methods.

Under aggressive optimized attacks, it achieves 98.8\% robot precision with 93.8\% recall and 98.3\% object precision with 95.4\% recall. In an occlusion-rich Webots warehouse, it maintains 92.5\% robot precision with 92.0\% recall and 97.3\% object precision with 85.0\% recall.

These results demonstrate joint improvements in the reliability and coverage of retained information.

summary.en: The paper presents NeST-Bayes for jointly inferring trust in robots and their reported object hypotheses in multi-robot systems. It uses inter-robot observation consistency to construct relational graphs, infer instantaneous trust evidence, and update trust beliefs over time with Bayesian updates. According to the abstract, it requires no preassigned trust, reputation data, or identity side channels. The authors report leading precision and recall on several benchmark measures, as well as results under optimized attacks and in an occlusion-rich Webots warehouse simulation.

In Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC), the control law is implicitly determined by the solution of an Optimal Control Problem (OCP).Consequently, OCP design is often tailored to specific platforms and tasks, demanding extensive expert knowledge and tuning effort.

To address this, we propose a unified NMPC framework that directly plans and controls the robot joints subject to task-space motion and force requirements and is capable of seamlessly generalizing across multiple robotic platforms and diverse tasks.

Furthermore, optimization-based methods often treat interactions as rigid contacts, making the torque solution sensitive to the modeling errors of the robot dynamics and the environment.

We study the intrinsic task-space impedance of our proposed controller, its partial contraction for differential stability and differential passivity under unmodeled interactions.

As a result, our framework enables closing the force-feedback loop in the high-level planning layer to achieve precise motion-force tracking performance, addressing the long-standing challenge of force-feedback NMPC.

Finally, we validate our framework on physical hardware, demonstrating hybrid motion-force control on a redundant manipulator and compliant locomotion on a quadruped, while preserving core NMPC advantages such as hard constraint satisfaction, optimal redundancy exploitation, and real-time planning under unforeseen interactions.

summary.en: The paper proposes a unified nonlinear model predictive control framework that directly plans and controls robot joints subject to task-space motion and force requirements. It studies the controller’s task-space impedance and stability properties under unmodeled interactions. The authors say the framework closes the force-feedback loop at the high-level planning layer for precise motion-force tracking. The abstract reports physical hardware validation: hybrid motion-force control on a redundant manipulator and compliant locomotion on a quadruped, while retaining hard-constraint satisfaction, redundancy exploitation, and real-time planning.

sections.text:
Changes in a robot's observations do not automatically imply changes in the task it is solving, but language-conditioned manipulation systems often fail to separate the two. If an object moves, for example, the locations at which actions should be executed may change while the underlying manipulation plan remains valid.

We introduce Sequential Planning via Anchored Robotic Keypoints (SPARK), which separates a task's symbolic plan from its execution-time perceptual grounding, and we experimentally isolate whether a fixed symbolic plan can survive substantial changes to the scene through execution-time re-grounding.

SPARK represents the task as a symbolic behavior tree whose object references are grounded to current 3D observations during execution, allowing the robot to update where actions are performed while preserving the plan. Runtime verification then enables local recovery and renewed grounding, only resorting to a new plan if necessary.

To test the separation between plan and perceptual-grounding, we perform a set of manipulation experiments with a fixed plan while moving objects during execution. Under a 10 cm displacement, verification and adaptation maintain 66.7pp task success, compared with 2.2pp when disabled, demonstrating the importance of the underlying principle.

Without task-specific model training, SPARK also achieves 72.6pp mean success across six LIBERO-PRO settings and 68pp across eleven physical task-embodiment settings on three robot platforms.

Together, these results show that robustness does not require re-planning the task and for an important class of failures, it is sufficient to preserve the plan and update the system's perception of a changing world. Code and videos can be found at https://cwru-aism.github.io/spark-page/

summary.en: SPARK separates a task’s symbolic plan from its execution-time perceptual grounding. It represents tasks as symbolic behavior trees, grounds object references in current 3D observations, and uses runtime verification for local recovery, replanning only if needed. In manipulation experiments that moved objects during execution, the authors report that with a 10 cm displacement, verification and adaptation maintained task success 66.7 percentage points higher than when disabled. Without task-specific model training, they also report mean success rates across six LIBERO-PRO settings and eleven physical task-embodiment settings on three robot platforms.

sections.text:
How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks.

Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference.

Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference.

We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks.

In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%.Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.

The authors report that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves success after conditioned pretraining. They introduce AXIS-Bench, built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations. In a real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raised success from 9.6% to 31.7%.

sections.text:
Zero-shot generalization to unseen embodiments is important for generalizable vision-language-action (VLA) models as robot hardware evolves and task-specific data collection remains costly.

However, a systematic understanding of this problem remains limited, in part because the literature lacks a unified zero-shot transfer definition and controlled evaluation settings that isolate embodiment changes from differences in tasks, scenes, or protocols.

To address this gap, we first distinguish strict zero-shot transfer, where the target embodiment is absent from all training data, from pretrain-exposed zero-shot transfer, where it appears only during pretraining. We then introduce a controlled benchmark spanning 14 held-out target embodiments across simulation and real-world validation.

Within this framework, we conduct a controlled analysis of four factors: state-action representations, pretraining embodiment diversity, auxiliary co-training objectives, and target-embodiment exposure.

Experimental results show that local end-effector (EEF) state-action representations, the source embodiment diversity, and auxiliary co-training improve cross-embodiment transfer by around 15, 18, and 7 percentage points, respectively.

We further find that adding only 5% target-embodiment data during pretraining improves average target-embodiment progress by 13.4 percentage points, showing that strict and pretrain-exposed zero-shot transfer are distinct and should be reported separately.

Together, these findings provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving cross-embodiment VLA transfer in stationary tabletop manipulation with two-finger grippers, while motivating future investigation of broader settings including mobile-base control, dexterous hands, and long-horizon tasks.

summary.en: The paper distinguishes strict zero-shot transfer, with no target embodiment in training, from pretrain-exposed transfer, where it appears only in pretraining. It introduces a controlled benchmark across 14 held-out embodiments, with simulation and real-world validation, and studies representations, embodiment diversity, co-training objectives, and target exposure. Experiments report transfer gains of around 15, 18, and 7 percentage points for three factors, and a 13.4-point progress gain from 5% target data in pretraining. Findings concern stationary tabletop manipulation with two-finger grippers.
summary.zh: 本文区分严格零样本迁移（目标机体未出现在任何训练数据中）与预训练暴露零样本迁移（目标机体仅在预训练中出现），并提出涵盖仿真和真实世界验证的受控基准。研究考察状态—动作表示、预训练机体多样性、辅助协同训练目标和目标机体暴露。实验显示，局部末端执行器表示、来源机体多样性和辅助协同训练分别带来约15、18和7个百分点的迁移提升；预训练中加入5%目标机体数据，使平均目标机体进度提升13.4个百分点。结论适用于静态桌面双指夹爪操作，并提出进一步研究更广泛场景。

sections.text:
Microsurgical anastomosis is one of the most challenging and sophisticated procedures for surgical robotics, requiring accurate manipulation of surgical instruments within a limited space to achieve precise operations.

Accurate surgical trajectory anticipation is essential for surgical scene understanding, intraoperative planning, robotic manipulation, and reliable behaviour analysis.

However, existing approaches mainly focus on features extracted from surgical videos and historical trajectories, while overlooking rich semantic and motion information that can provide more discriminative multi-modal representations for complex surgical instrument-tissue interactions.

In this work, we propose a cross-modal feature fusion framework for long-term 2D and 3D microsurgical anastomosis trajectory anticipation. The proposed framework consists of a multi-modal representation extractor and a cross-modal feature fusion network.

Semantic recognition of surgical objects and consecutive motion estimation are incorporated as multi-modal visual cues, providing complementary spatial and temporal guidance for instrument-tissue interaction characterization.

A coarse-to-fine progressive fusion strategy with a long-short-term memory mechanism is introduced to capture temporal dependencies step by step. The training and evaluation are conducted on our established robotic platform and a comprehensive dataset containing both phantom and ex-vivo surgical scenarios is constructed.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods and exhibits improved robustness across different surgical scenes, highlighting its potential for both intelligent robot-assisted and autonomous surgical systems.

summary.en: The paper proposes cross-modal feature fusion for long-term 2D and 3D trajectory anticipation in microsurgical anastomosis. Its framework combines semantic recognition of surgical objects with consecutive motion estimation, then uses coarse-to-fine progressive fusion and an LSTM mechanism to capture temporal dependencies. Training and evaluation use the authors’ robotic platform and a dataset containing phantom and ex-vivo scenarios. The authors report that quantitative and qualitative experiments consistently outperform existing methods and show improved robustness across surgical scenes.

Numerous locomotion controllers have been designed based on Reinforcement Learning (RL) to facilitate blind quadrupedal locomotion traversing challenging terrains. Nevertheless, locomotion control is still a challenging task for quadruped robots traversing diverse terrains amidst unforeseen disturbances.

Recently, privileged learning has been employed to learn reliable and robust quadrupedal locomotion over various terrains based on a teacher-student architecture. However, its one-encoder structure is not adequate in addressing external force perturbations.

The student policy would experience inevitable performance degradation due to the feature embedding discrepancy between the feature encoder of the teacher policy and the one of the student policy.

Hence, this paper presents a privileged learning framework with multiple feature encoders and a residual policy network for robust and reliable quadruped locomotion subject to various external perturbations.

The multi-encoder structure can decouple latent features from different privileged information, ultimately leading to enhanced performance of the learned policy in terms of robustness, stability, and reliability. The efficiency of the proposed feature encoding module is analyzed in depth using extensive simulation data.

The introduction of the residual policy network helps mitigate the performance degradation experienced by the student policy that attempts to clone the behaviors of a teacher policy.

The proposed framework is evaluated on a Unitree GO1 robot, showcasing its performance enhancement over the state-of-the-art privileged learning algorithm through extensive experiments conducted on diverse terrains. Ablation studies are conducted to illustrate the efficiency of the residual policy network.

summary.en: The paper presents a privileged-learning framework for quadruped locomotion under external perturbations, using multiple feature encoders and a residual policy network. The authors say the encoders separate latent features from different privileged information to improve robustness, stability, and reliability, while the residual network mitigates student-policy degradation when cloning a teacher. The encoding module is analyzed with simulation data. The framework is evaluated on a Unitree GO1 across diverse terrains and compared with a state-of-the-art privileged-learning algorithm; ablation studies examine the residual network.

Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, \omega)$ and realized motion.

Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms.

First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers.

Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions.

Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.

Wheel odometry provides an efficient motion prior for ground robots but is prone to transient violations such as wheel slip or terrain-induced tilt. In filtering-based odometry, these violations frequently trigger divergence when they coincide with constrained geometric observability (e.g., featureless corridors).

We address this challenge by proposing ToF-Wheel Odometry (TWO), a tightly-coupled filtering framework that integrates wheel kinematics with geometric constraints from Time-of-Flight (ToF) cameras.

The primary contribution of this work is a degeneracy-aware, directional covariance-shaping strategy that replaces heuristic online covariance tuning with geometry-conditioned inflation. The core idea is to infer process noise from geometric corrections with a strict reliability check.

We decompose the posterior-to-prior correction into a wheel-explainable subspace and an orthogonal remainder.

The process covariance is anisotropically adjusted according to the observability of the ToF update: if the geometry is degenerate in non-kinematic directions, the remainder is suppressed as sensor noise; if the geometry is distinct, it is admitted as a valid kinematic violation.

Additionally, we introduce an intra-frame feedback loop that retrospectively repairs the process covariance within the current frame to reduce structural lag during bursty disturbances.

Extensive experiments on challenging scenarios demonstrate that TWO improves trajectory accuracy and robustness compared to static and adaptive Gaussian filtering, robustly navigating the trade-off between kinematic reliability and limited sensing capabilities.

Collaborative planning under operational constraints is essential for heterogeneous robot teams in large-scale missions. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) provide rapid area coverage but are limited by onboard energy, while Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) can serve as mobile recharging stations yet are constrained by road-network traversability.

Effective collaboration must enforce operational constraints during execution while enabling parallel, coordinated actions.

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have shown promise through token unmasking but have two key limitations: entropy-guided scheduling assumes distributional alignment and reliance on differentiable constraints for diffusion-time optimization.

We propose Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion (MEND), which formulates collaborative planning as a conditional masked generative process to generate context-aware action sequences for UAV-UGV teams.

MEND introduces a neuro-symbolic diffusion paradigm that constrains conditional masked diffusion policies at execution by reweighting the learned action distribution with a logic-induced admissibility indicator, thereby enforcing compliance with operational constraints.

MEND introduces an error-bounded inference scheduling at execution that constructs the unmasking schedule by selecting positions with minimal predictive entropy over the constraint-aware action distribution, enhancing collaborative planning optimality under operational constraints.

Extensive experimental results in simulation, on real-world maps, and with physical robot teams demonstrate that MEND advances UAV-UGV collaborative planning under operational constraints.

Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images.

We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments.

Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling.

Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action.

Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow.

To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction.

After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction.

Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.

Some deep learning-based point cloud registration methods struggle with zero-shot generalization, often requiring target-domain retraining, fine-tuning, or dataset-specific metric parameter tuning for new environments.

We identify three critical limitations: (a) fixed user-defined parameters (e.g., voxel size, search radius) that fail to generalize across varying scales, (b) learned keypoint detectors exhibit poor cross-domain transferability, and (c) absolute coordinates amplify scale mismatches between datasets.

To address these three issues, we present BUFFER-X, a registration framework whose descriptor model is trained once and then applied without parameter tuning or target-domain retraining, which achieves zero-shot generalization through: (a) geometric bootstrapping for automatic hyperparameter estimation, (b) distribution-aware farthest point sampling to replace learned detectors, and (c) patch-level coordinate normalization to ensure scale consistency.

For efficiency-critical applications, we present BUFFER-X-Lite from a holistic system perspective, integrating the BUFFER-X front-end and adaptive early exit with the fast and robust pose solver to reduce total computation time by 43% relative to BUFFER-X while preserving comparable accuracy.

Language models trained with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning can generalize knowledge through reasoning, express precise actions, and pursue goals over many steps, raising the ceiling on what an embodied agent can understand and decide. Physical interaction, however, remains the domain of action policies, which provide dense, low-latency control.

We present NavGPT-3, a harness that connects the two models, with an OS-like runtime built above it: reasoning, acting, and monitoring run as threads with their own context, tools, and permissions, while the runtime schedules them and decides which thread controls the robot's motion, so that the robot can react to sudden real-world events through interruption and thread switching.

Beneath it, our action policy NavGPT VLA, trained on 19.28M examples, allocates visual tokens using codec allocation, in proportion to scene change; its 8B model alone reaches 76.94 SR on R2R-CE and leads RxR-CE with 82.39 SR.

These results show that designing this embodied interface is central to connecting frontier language-model intelligence with low-level physical control. We will release all models, code, and evaluation records.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models inherit powerful semantic representations from large language models, but carrying over their design priorities can leave the demands of physical control under-specified. Stable manipulation requires high-frequency proprioceptive feedback and persistent motor state, in addition to instruction understanding.

Here we introduce Neuromorphic Vision-Language-Action (NeuroVLA), a brain-inspired architecture that couples a cortical vision-language planner to recurrent cerebellar modulation and a stateful spiking spinal controller.

These components translate semantic intent into actions while incorporating high-frequency proprioceptive and force feedback, maintaining short-term motor memory, and enabling local responses to unexpected contact.

Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change.

Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state.

TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence.

This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes.

From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.

In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.

Nearest-neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on $SO（2）$ or $SO（3）$ and poses on $SE（2）$ or $SE（3）$, and a Euclidean KD-tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors.

We present a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact NN search on user-defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds ($\mathbb{R}^n$, $SO（2）$, $SO（3）$, $S^n$; products $SE（2）$, $SE（3）$, tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap-aware for circular coordinates and double-cover-aware for unit quaternions.

Experiments confirm exactness (recall $1.0$ vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean-on-raw shortcut collapses to recall $\approx 0.5^{m}$ for $m$ rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force.

We further contribute an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding-window LiDAR maps) or $SE（3）$ trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail-latency-bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann

Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical.

We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap.

Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy.

We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks.

Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation.

Generalist robot manipulation policies have developed rapidly, yet their reliable evaluation remains challenging due to fundamental flaws in existing simulation benchmarks: prominent sim-to-real gaps, narrow task coverage, and unfair evaluation caused by ambiguous training-test pipelines.

Prior works only partially resolve these issues and lack simultaneous faithfulness, diversity, and fairness, while static benchmark designs fail to sustain long-term policy development. X2Real offers a faithful, diverse, and fair evolving evaluation infrastructure, effectively bridging the sim-to-real evaluation gap and supporting the advancement of generalist robotic manipulation policies.

Recent advances in zero-shot voice cloning systems make it possible to reproduce a recognizable voice from a short recording and attach it to arbitrary virtual characters. Prior work suggests that familiar vocal identity can carry over associated personality impressions to new targets such as robots or virtual characters.

However, these works have mainly examined familiarity and personalization effects rather than directly testing whether a cloned familiar voice systematically transfers personality impressions to an embodied virtual character.

Such transference raises the concern that cloned voices could be used to manipulate people into engaging with virtual characters as capable social actors. Across two studies, we investigated whether personality impressions transfer when a virtual character speaks with the cloned voice of a familiar person.

Study 1 examined this question in a real-world university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer familiar to the participating students. Study 2 examined the same question online using voices of social media content creators and members of their communities.

Drawing on the concepts of identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction, we show that evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies. Observed effects were selective and did not generalize across traits or study contexts.

In the online study in particular, recognizable voice identity cues activated expectations about the speaker but did not reconstruct the broader person impression. Qualitative responses further indicated that judgments were frequently shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together.

Our findings moderate common concerns that cloned voices straightforwardly manipulate people into perceiving artificial characters as capable social actors.
